title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM JOSHUA’S FIRST BATTLE
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM JOSHUA’S FIRST BATTLE
There are battles that change history.
Then there are battles that change the human heart.

Most believers know the story of Jericho. They remember the walls. They remember the marching. They remember the victory. But buried beneath the noise of collapsing stone is a lesson so personal, so deeply transformative, that many of us miss it entirely.
Because Joshua’s first battle was never really about Jericho.
For years, Joshua had lived in the shadow of giants.

He had watched Egypt crumble beneath God’s judgment. He had crossed the Red Sea on dry ground. He had wandered through wilderness seasons that tested the faith of an entire generation. He had stood beside Moses, one of the greatest leaders in human history.
The responsibility rested on Joshua’s shoulders.
The future of an entire nation stood before him.
The city represented everything that stood between God's people and God's promise.
Joshua could not negotiate with it.
And maybe that is exactly where God wanted him.
Because God often brings us to situations where our strength becomes irrelevant.
Before the battle began, Joshua experienced one of the most profound encounters recorded in Scripture.
“When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man stood before him with his drawn sword in his hand.”
“Are you for us, or for our adversaries?”
“No; but as commander of the army of the LORD I have now come.”
The Hebrew phrase used here is:
Joshua asks which side God is on.
The Commander does not answer that question.
Instead, He reveals a greater reality.
The issue was never whether God was on Joshua’s side.
The issue was whether Joshua was on God’s side.
Many of us still ask Joshua’s question.
“God, are You helping me achieve what I want?”
But God continually redirects us toward a deeper question.
Everything changed when Joshua realized who stood before him.
“Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped.”
The Hebrew word translated worship is:

“To bow low.”
“To prostrate oneself.”
“To completely submit before authority.”
And that is the lesson that shattered me.
Before God gave Joshua a battle plan, God required Joshua’s surrender.
Before the victory came the kneeling.
Before the walls fell the pride had to fall.
The modern church often reverses the order.
But God has never operated that way.
The kingdom advances through surrendered hearts.
Joshua's strategy would have sounded absurd to every military expert in the ancient world.
Because God wanted the victory to be undeniably His.
The Apostle Paul would later write:
God is not opposed to strength.
The greatest obstacle standing before Joshua was not the wall.
It was the temptation to trust himself.
And if we are honest, that remains our struggle too.
Many of us are facing our own Jerichos.
A secret sin nobody knows about.
We stare at the walls and calculate our chances.
Meanwhile God is asking a completely different question.
The Hebrew word often translated “trust” throughout Scripture carries the idea of confident reliance and secure dependence.
Joshua learned that God’s power becomes most visible when human confidence reaches its limit.
That lesson becomes even more powerful when viewed through the lens of Jesus Christ.
Joshua led people into an earthly inheritance.
Jesus leads believers into an eternal inheritance.
Jesus defeated sin, death, and hell.
Jesus opens the way into the Kingdom of God.
The story ultimately points beyond Joshua.
And nowhere is this clearer than at the cross.
That has always been God’s pattern.
The woman caught in adultery was condemned by society.
The thief on the cross was dying under judgment.
And perhaps most importantly for many reading this right now—
your story is not finished either.
Maybe you carry regrets you wish you could erase.
Maybe there are chapters of your life you hope nobody ever discovers.
The Gospel does not deny those chapters.
The Greek word for grace is:
Divine kindness bestowed upon the undeserving.
That is not merely a theological concept.
That is the story of every believer.
Grace is God meeting people where they are and refusing to leave them there.
Grace takes shattered pieces and creates something beautiful.
Grace takes failures and creates testimonies.
Grace takes sinners and creates saints.
Grace takes scandal and writes redemption.
The lesson I learned from Joshua’s first battle is simple but life-changing.
The greatest victories are not won through human strength.
They are won through surrendered hearts.
Jericho fell because Joshua first fell on his face before God.
And perhaps the breakthrough you are praying for begins in exactly the same place.
Not with another attempt to manage everything yourself.
Maybe today God is not asking you to fight harder.
Maybe He is asking you to kneel.
What wall are you trusting God to bring down?
Your support helps expand Gospel-centered ministry, reach more souls, create more faith-building content, and glorify God through the spreading of His truth.
Because one surrendered heart can become the beginning of another person’s miracle.
